issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: 'My body has been permanently damaged by what happened' implies an enduring physical injury theme, but the rest of the selected items do not support a bodily injury-focused combat presentation: memory items emphasize fragmentation/unreality, triggers emphasize intrusion/power imbalance, and strategies emphasize avoidance/hypervigilance rather than injury management. This appraisal is insufficiently anchored in the rest of the profile.

vignette: Malia Tui was 22 years old, a combat medic deployed with a Marine unit in Vietnam, when the helicopter she was aboard took heavy fire during a medical evacuation. She remembers the rotor blades snarling overhead, the crew chief shouting, the wounded soldier beside her whose hand she was gripping, and then the ground rushing up as the aircraft lurched and spun. The next hours come back to her only in disconnected pieces: the smell of hydraulic fluid, the sound of her own breath, the sensation of being pinned beneath a seat while someone yelled about incoming. Even now, forty-four years later, the memory feels so extreme that she sometimes struggles to believe it really happened to her, and when she tries to describe it to anyone, she finds she cannot find the words-the pieces simply will not fit into a coherent story. That single event reshaped her life. After returning home, Malia discovered that the sound of a helicopter, even on television, would suddenly and involuntarily yank her back into those fragmented moments, the rotor noise acting as a direct cue for the disorienting flash of images and sensations. This connection between the external trigger and the intrusion of the memory became so reliable that she began to dread any situation where she might hear an aircraft, and she came to believe that she had to be on guard all the time, scanning the sky and her surroundings for signs of threat. The hypervigilance, in turn, fed her isolation: she felt set apart from neighbors who had never served, and she doubted her own judgment, convinced she could not trust herself to do the right thing if something went wrong. These negative appraisals of herself and the world made her more sensitive to any hint of danger, so that even the everyday power imbalance of a meeting with her supervisor-someone who held authority over her-would spike her anxiety, triggering a fresh wave of the fragmented memory and reinforcing her sense of helplessness. To manage this, Malia developed a set of strategies that, while intended to protect her, ultimately deepened the problem. She stopped going out unless absolutely necessary, and when she did leave her apartment, she always made sure to stay close to an exit, positioning herself so she could leave quickly if needed. Avoiding strong emotions became a rule-she would tense up if she felt sadness or anger rising, because allowing herself to feel fully seemed to dissolve the boundary between present and past, sending the memory pieces swirling back. This avoidance of feelings, however, only made the memory more intrusive when it did break through; without emotional processing, the disconnected fragments remained raw and vivid. At work as a curriculum designer, she found that sitting in a windowless conference room during staff meetings activated her sense of being trapped, and her habit of choosing the chair nearest the door became so ingrained that colleagues noticed and commented, which only increased her sense of being isolated and different. The hypervigilance she carried into those meetings-watching who entered, where the exits were-also primed her to perceive any disagreement from a senior colleague as a power imbalance, instantly triggering the memory of being pinned and helpless. Over the years, these patterns tightened into a self-reinforcing cycle. The more she avoided going out, the more isolated she felt, and the more she doubted her capacity to handle everyday situations. That self-doubt made her even more alert to potential threats, and her constant scanning for exits or helicopter sounds meant she was always on the lookout, which paradoxically made triggers more likely to capture her attention. When a trigger did occur-a distant helicopter, a domineering voice in a meeting-the memory would surface with its disjointed, unreal quality, and she would immediately clamp down on her emotions, staying near an exit, which in turn prevented her from challenging the belief that the world was dangerous and she was not competent. "Because the memory itself remained so disjointed and overwhelming, she began to see traces of it everywhere-in the quality of winter light, in the sound of a chair scraping the floor, in any sudden silence-so that everyday moments now carried the weight of potential re-entry into that fragmented space." The end result was that her strategies actively fed the very memory and negative appraisals they were meant to suppress. At sixty-six, Malia has become weary of the vigilance and the narrowing of her life. She recently retired from full-time work, but the loss of her daily structure has left her with more time to ruminate, and the helicopter sounds from a nearby hospital's air ambulance have become an almost daily trigger. What finally brought her to seek help was a moment in a grocery store when a loud air conditioner hum sounded exactly like a rotor whine; she froze in the aisle, her heart pounding, and for several seconds she was back in the wrecked helicopter, unable to move or speak. The shame of that public episode, combined with her growing fear that she can no longer manage on her own, has pushed her to find a therapist. She is most afraid that talking about the event will make the fragments worse, but she is also hoping-tentatively-that someone might help her put the pieces together at last.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not contain a causal relationship where the memory (intrusive memory) leads to the occurrence or increased perception of triggers; instead, triggers cause the memory, and strategies cause trigger detection.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not contain a causal relationship where the memory (intrusive memory) leads to the occurrence or increased perception of triggers; instead, triggers cause the memory, and strategies cause trigger detection.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
